h1: Washing beer glasses by hand without leaving a soapy film
title: Hand washing beer glasses without film | Craft Beer School
desc: How to hand wash beer glasses so foam holds and bubbles do not cling to the sides: the right detergent, the rinse and how to dry them.
teaser: If bubbles cling to the side of your glass and the head vanishes in a minute, the glass is the problem, not the beer.
standfirst: A glass can look spotless and still kill a beer's head. The culprit is usually a thin film of detergent, grease or lint. Here is how to wash glasses by hand so they come out beer clean.
sections: What a dirty glass does to beer

Foam is a network of bubbles held together by proteins and hop compounds. Fat and detergent residue break that network. Pour a good lager into a glass with a trace of oil or soap and the head collapses fast. You also see bubbles clinging to the sides of the glass, because tiny specks of residue give carbon dioxide somewhere to gather.

A beer clean glass does the opposite. Foam lasts, the beer leaves rings of lace down the glass as you drink and the bubbles rise in fine streams from the bottom rather than sticking to the walls. Our guide to the beer clean glass test shows how to check.
Keep beer glasses apart from everything else

The single best habit is to wash beer glasses on their own. A sink that has just held a pan with ghee or a plate with butter chicken leaves a greasy layer in the water. Every glass you wash after that picks some up.

Wash beer glasses first, in fresh hot water, before the dinner plates. Keep a dedicated sponge or soft brush for them that never touches a frying pan. Do not use glasses that have held milk, lassi or oily drinks for beer unless you have washed them twice. These sound fussy, but they cost nothing once they are routine.
Use a little of the right detergent

Most people use far too much washing up liquid. A few drops in a full sink is enough. Unscented liquids are better than lemon or herbal ones, because perfume can linger on glass. Avoid detergents that advertise added moisturisers or softeners: they are designed to leave something on the surface, which is exactly what you do not want.

Wash in water as hot as your hands allow, around 45 °C. Scrub the inside of the glass all the way to the bottom. Lipstick and lip balm are oily, so give the rim extra attention. A tall weizen glass may need a bottle brush to reach the base.
The rinse matters more than the wash

Soapy film comes from poor rinsing, not from poor washing. Rinse each glass under clean running water, inside and out, until there is no slippery feel left. Then give it a final rinse in cold water.

If your tap water is hard, as borewell water often is in parts of India, minerals can leave white spots as the glass dries. Spots are harmless but they can affect foam. A final rinse in filtered or RO water solves it. Every few weeks, scrub glasses with a paste of baking soda and water, then rinse well, to lift any film that has built up.
Dry them in the air, not with a towel

Tea towels carry lint, grease from hands and whatever else they wiped last. Drying a beer glass with one undoes the wash. Stand glasses upside down on a rack or a ridged drying mat so air can get inside and water can drain.

Do not stand them rim down on a flat cloth or a solid surface. Moisture trapped inside can leave a musty smell, especially in humid monsoon months. Store dry glasses upright in a closed cupboard away from the stove, so cooking fumes do not settle on them.

Some glasses are harder to clean than others. A tall weizen glass or a narrow stange is hard to reach with a sponge, so residue builds up at the base. A bottle brush with soft bristles solves it. Stemmed tulips and goblets have a curved bowl where film collects under the lip.

Etched glasses, the ones with a small logo or pattern scratched into the base, are made to release a steady stream of bubbles from that spot. Scrubbing them hard with an abrasive pad can damage the etching. Use a soft brush there.

Plastic and acrylic glasses scratch easily and hold onto oil more than glass does. If you use them outdoors, wash them on their own and replace them once they look cloudy. Old plastic is very hard to get beer clean, however careful you are.

Wet a clean glass and look at it. Water should sheet evenly over the surface. If it breaks into droplets and patches, there is still grease on the glass. Another quick check: sprinkle a little salt inside a wet glass. Salt sticks evenly to a clean glass and leaves gaps where there is film.

Then pour a beer. You want a steady head, fine bubbles rising from the base and lace that marks each sip down the glass. A head that lasts two or three minutes on a pale lager is a good sign.

Tonight, wash your beer glasses first, in fresh water, with two drops of unscented detergent. Rinse twice and leave them upside down on a rack. Pour your next beer into one of them and the difference in the head will tell you whether your old routine was the problem.
faqs: Why do bubbles stick to the side of my beer glass?
Residue on the glass, such as detergent, grease or lint, gives carbon dioxide a place to collect. A beer clean glass lets bubbles rise from the bottom instead.
Can I put beer glasses in a dishwasher?
You can, but rinse aid and grease from other dishes can leave a film. Many beer drinkers prefer to hand wash and air dry their glasses.
Should I dry beer glasses with a towel?
No. Towels leave lint and grease. Air dry glasses upside down on a rack.
What detergent is best for beer glasses?
A small amount of plain, unscented washing up liquid, rinsed off thoroughly, works for home use.
